questions.explanation: 1. Qf4# is a dovetail mate: the Queen, protected by the King on g3, covers f5, f6, g4, h4 and h6, while Black's pawns on g6 and h5 block the last two squares.
questions.hintText: The Queen needs a square next to the King where your own King protects her.

questions.question: White to move: the Bishop on c4 controls g8 and the g7-pawn boxes in its own King. Find Greco's mate in 1!
questions.explanation: 1. Qh5# is Greco's mate: the Queen checks along the h-file, the Bishop on c4 guards g8, and the pawn on g7 blocks the King's last square.
questions.hintText: The only open line next to the King is the file at the edge of the board.

questions.question: White to move: Black's Rook and Bishop stand right behind their King. Deliver the swallow's-tail mate in 1!
questions.explanation: 1. Qe6# is a swallow's-tail mate: the Queen, protected by the pawn on d5, covers d6, f6, d7, f7 and e8, and Black's Rook on d8 and Bishop on f8 block the remaining squares.
questions.hintText: Look for a Queen check that your pawn supports.

questions.question: White to move: the Rook already controls the g-file. Deliver Morphy's mate in 1!
questions.explanation: 1. Bf6# is Morphy's mate: the Bishop checks on the long diagonal, the Rook on g1 covers g7 and g8, and the pawn on h7 blocks its own King.
questions.hintText: The King cannot step onto the g-file: look for a check that cannot be blocked.

questions.question: It is Black's turn. Black is not in check but has no legal move. What is the result of the game?
questions.optionsString: White wins|Black wins|Draw by stalemate|Black skips the move
questions.explanation: This is stalemate: the player to move has no legal move and is not in check, so the game is drawn at once.
questions.hintText: Not being in check is the key detail: this is not checkmate.

questions.question: After how many consecutive moves by each side without a capture or a pawn move may a player claim a draw?
questions.explanation: Under the fifty-move rule a player may claim a draw once 50 moves by each side have passed without a capture or a pawn move.
questions.hintText: The rule is named after this number of moves.

questions.question: How many times must the same position occur, with the same player to move, before a player may claim a draw by repetition?
questions.explanation: A player may claim a draw when the same position, with the same player to move and the same possible moves, appears for the third time. It need not happen on consecutive moves.
questions.hintText: The repetitions need not be consecutive; think of the usual name of this rule.

questions.question: An enemy pawn has just advanced two squares and landed beside your pawn. When may you capture it en passant?
questions.optionsString: Only on your very next move|On any of your next three moves|Any time before that pawn moves again|Only if the capture gives check
questions.explanation: En passant is allowed only on the move immediately after the enemy pawn's double step. If you play something else, the right is lost.
questions.hintText: The French name means 'in passing': the chance does not wait.

questions.question: A pawn reaches the last rank. Which pieces may it be promoted to?
questions.optionsString: Only a queen|Any piece already captured|Queen, rook, bishop or knight|Any piece, even a second king
questions.explanation: The player chooses a queen, rook, bishop or knight of the same colour. It does not matter which pieces have been captured, so a second queen is fine.
questions.hintText: The choice does not depend on which pieces have left the board, but one piece is unique.

questions.question: Which tactic is it when a single piece attacks two or more enemy pieces at the same time?
questions.explanation: A fork is a double attack by one piece; the opponent can usually save only one of the attacked pieces. Knights are famous for it.
questions.hintText: The name comes from a tool with two or more prongs.

questions.question: A Rook checks the enemy King; the King steps aside and the Rook captures the Queen that stood behind it on the same line. What is this tactic called?
questions.explanation: In a skewer the more valuable piece is in front: it must move away and the piece behind it is lost. In a pin it is the other way round.
questions.hintText: It is the reverse of a pin: the more valuable piece stands in front.

questions.question: What do you call a pawn that has no enemy pawns in front of it on its own file or on the two adjacent files?
questions.explanation: A passed pawn cannot be stopped or captured by enemy pawns on its way to promotion, so pieces have to hold it back.
questions.hintText: No enemy pawn can block it or capture it on its way to the last rank.

questions.question: What does the notation 'O-O-O' stand for in a game score?
questions.optionsString: Kingside castling|A draw by agreement|Queenside castling|Three checks in a row
questions.explanation: O-O-O is queenside (long) castling: the King goes to the c-file and the Rook to the d-file. Kingside castling is written O-O.
questions.hintText: On one wing there are more squares between King and Rook: that wing gets the extra 'O'.

questions.question: In chess annotation, what does the symbol '?!' after a move mean?
questions.optionsString: A brilliant move|An interesting move|A blunder|A dubious move
questions.explanation: '?!' marks a dubious move: probably not best, but not a clear mistake. The reverse, '!?', marks an interesting move.
questions.hintText: The first sign carries the main verdict; the second one softens it.

questions.question: Which of these can never checkmate a lone King, even if the defender plays the worst possible moves?
questions.optionsString: King and rook|King and knight|King and queen|King and pawn
questions.explanation: King and one knight (or one bishop) cannot build any mating position, so the game is drawn at once. A pawn can still promote.
questions.hintText: With one of these there is no mating position at all, however badly the defender plays.

questions.question: Which of these does NOT make castling illegal?
questions.optionsString: The King is in check|The King has moved before|The King would cross an attacked square|The Rook is under attack
questions.explanation: Only the King's squares matter: it may not be in check, and may not pass over or land on an attacked square. An attacked Rook can still take part in castling.
questions.hintText: The restrictions about attacks concern only one of the two castling pieces.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'win the exchange'?
questions.optionsString: To win a rook for a bishop or knight|To trade queens when ahead in material|To swap a bishop for a knight|To win a pawn in a series of trades
questions.explanation: 'The exchange' is the difference in value between a rook and a minor piece. Winning it means giving a bishop or knight and getting a rook.
questions.hintText: It is about trading two pieces of unequal value: one of them is a minor piece.

questions.question: A player forces a draw with an endless series of checks that the opponent cannot escape. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Perpetual check leads to a draw, in practice by threefold repetition or by agreement, because the checked King can never get away.
questions.hintText: The checks never stop, and the name says so.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'make luft' for your castled King?
questions.optionsString: Move a pawn to give the King a flight square|Lift a rook in front of the King's pawns|Trade the bishop that guards the King|Run the King towards the centre
questions.explanation: 'Luft' is German for 'air': a pawn move such as h3 or g3 gives the King an escape square and prevents back-rank mates.
questions.hintText: 'Luft' means 'air': what does a King stuck behind its own pawns need?

questions.question: How must a double check always be answered?
questions.optionsString: By capturing one of the checking pieces|By blocking one of the checks|By a counter-check|By moving the King
questions.explanation: Two pieces give check at once, so capturing or blocking can deal with only one of them. The only legal reply is a King move.
questions.hintText: One move cannot capture or block two attackers at the same time.

questions.question: Which opening moves define the Queen's Gambit?
questions.explanation: The Queen's Gambit is 1. d4 d5 2. c4: White offers the c-pawn to draw Black's d-pawn away from the centre. 1. e4 e5 2. f4 is the King's Gambit.
questions.hintText: White offers a pawn on the queenside to undermine Black's pawn in the centre.

questions.question: In the Lucena position, where does the stronger side's King stand?
questions.optionsString: Behind its pawn, on the 6th rank|On the queening square, in front of its pawn|Beside its pawn, on the 7th rank|Cut off, two files from its pawn
questions.explanation: In the Lucena position the pawn is on the 7th rank and its King stands on the queening square in front of it, with the defending King cut off. The Rook then builds a bridge to let the King out.
questions.hintText: The pawn is on the 7th rank and cannot advance yet: what is in its way?

questions.question: White has a King on e6 and a pawn on e5; Black has a King on e8. No other pieces. What is the result with best play?
questions.optionsString: White wins only if White is to move|White wins only if Black is to move|White wins whoever is to move|Draw whoever is to move
questions.explanation: A King on the 6th rank in front of its pawn (not a rook's pawn) always wins. With White to move: 1. Kd6 Kd8 2. e6 Ke8 3. e7 Kf7 4. Kd7; with Black to move the white King simply outflanks.
questions.hintText: The King already stands on a key square of its pawn; check whether the move matters.

questions.question: In King and pawn versus King, which pawn gives the fewest winning chances because the defender only needs to reach the corner?
questions.optionsString: A centre pawn (d or e)|A bishop's pawn (c or f)|A knight's pawn (b or g)|A rook's pawn (a or h)
questions.explanation: With a rook's pawn there is no room to outflank: once the defending King reaches the queening corner, every winning attempt ends in stalemate.
questions.hintText: Outflanking needs room on both sides of the pawn.

questions.question: White has a pawn on a5; Black's King is on e5 and White's King is too far away to help. Can Black's King catch the pawn?
questions.optionsString: Yes, whoever is to move|Only if Black is to move|Only if White is to move|No, whoever is to move
questions.explanation: The pawn's square runs from a5 to a8 and across to d8 and d5. With Black to move the King steps into it (1... Kd6) and catches the pawn; after 1. a6 the square shrinks to a6-c8-c6 and the King is too late.
questions.hintText: Draw the square from the pawn to its queening square, then see who moves first.

questions.question: With King, knight and a dark-squared bishop against a lone King, in which corners can checkmate be forced?
questions.optionsString: a1 and h8|a8 and h1|In any corner|Only in h8
questions.explanation: Mate with bishop and knight can only be forced in a corner of the bishop's colour. The dark corners are a1 and h8.
questions.hintText: The bishop must be able to attack the corner square itself.

questions.question: Can King and two knights force checkmate against a lone King?
questions.optionsString: Yes, within about 20 moves|Yes, but only in a corner|No, no mating position exists|No, mate cannot be forced
questions.explanation: Mating positions with two knights do exist, but the defender can always avoid them: the attacker would have to release a stalemate first. With correct defence it is a draw.
questions.hintText: Try to weave the mating net: what happens one move before the mate?

questions.question: Which piece is regarded as the ideal blockader of a passed pawn, as Aron Nimzowitsch taught in 'My System'?
questions.explanation: A knight in front of a passed pawn loses none of its power: it attacks squares past the pawn and is hard to drive away. Rooks and queens are wasted on blockade duty.
questions.hintText: It is the piece whose moves are not obstructed by the pawn it blocks.

questions.question: What is the aim of a minority attack, for example White's b4-b5 in the Carlsbad structure?
questions.optionsString: To open the centre for the bishops|To create a pawn weakness in the majority|To win space for a kingside attack|To trade off all the queenside pawns
questions.explanation: Fewer pawns advance against more: after b4-b5 and an exchange on c6 Black is left with a backward or isolated pawn that White's pieces can attack.
questions.hintText: Two pawns attack three: think about what Black's pawns look like after the exchange.

questions.question: According to Nimzowitsch, where should a pawn chain be attacked?
questions.optionsString: At its head|In the middle|At its base|From the flank
questions.explanation: The base is the rearmost pawn of the chain, the one that no other pawn protects. If it falls, the pawns in front of it lose their support.
questions.hintText: Find the one pawn in the chain that no other pawn defends.

questions.question: Why is an outside passed pawn such a strong asset in a pawn endgame?
questions.optionsString: It can never be captured by a King|It promotes with check on the long diagonal|It gives its owner the opposition|It lures the enemy King away from the other pawns
questions.explanation: The defending King must leave to stop the distant pawn. Meanwhile the other King walks to the remaining pawns and wins them.
questions.hintText: Stopping it takes time: where is the defending King when the other pawns are attacked?

questions.question: What does the 'principle of two weaknesses' advise the side with an advantage to do?
questions.optionsString: Trade pieces until only two pawns remain|Attack the same weakness with two pieces|Create a second target far from the first one|Keep two pawn islands instead of three
questions.explanation: One weakness can usually be defended. A second target on another part of the board stretches the defence until it cannot cover both.
questions.hintText: A defender can guard one target; think about what overstretches the defence.

questions.question: Which pieces deliver the final checkmate in Légal's Mate, after White has let the Queen be captured?
questions.optionsString: Queen and knight|Two knights and a bishop|Two rooks|Rook and bishop
questions.explanation: After 5. Nxe5 Bxd1 the minor pieces finish the job: 6. Bxf7+ Ke7 7. Nd5#. The bishop and the two knights cover every square around the King.
questions.hintText: White's attack starts by ignoring a pin on the f3-knight.

questions.question: In the combination known as Philidor's Legacy, which piece is sacrificed next to the enemy King to force a smothered mate?
questions.explanation: After a double check the Queen is sacrificed on g8 (Qg8+!). The Rook must capture, and Nf7# is a smothered mate.
questions.hintText: The sacrificed piece gives check from next to the King, and only a Rook can capture it.

questions.question: Who won the 'Immortal Game' of 1851 by sacrificing both rooks and the queen?
questions.explanation: Adolf Anderssen beat Lionel Kieseritzky in London in 1851, giving up a bishop, both rooks and the queen to mate with his minor pieces.
questions.hintText: The German winner also won the London 1851 tournament.

questions.question: What is the usual reason for promoting a pawn to a rook instead of a queen?
questions.optionsString: To avoid stalemating the opponent|To give check from a safer distance|To keep the fifty-move count running|To stop the new piece being pinned
questions.explanation: A rook is enough to win, but controls fewer squares than a queen. When a new queen would leave the opponent without a legal move, the rook avoids the stalemate.
questions.hintText: Sometimes the new piece can control too many squares.

questions.question: In King and pawn versus King, the attacker's King stands on the 6th rank beside its centre pawn, which now advances to the 7th; the defending King is on the back rank. According to the classic rule, when does the attacker win?
questions.optionsString: If the pawn advances without check|If the pawn advances with check|Always, whatever the position|Never, it is always stalemate
questions.explanation: If the pawn reaches the 7th rank without check, the defending King must give way and the pawn queens. If it arrives with check, the King steps in front of it and the attacker must give stalemate or lose the pawn.
questions.hintText: After the pawn move, ask whose turn it is and whether that King has a good square.

questions.question: Under FIDE rules, after how many moves by each side without a capture or pawn move is the game drawn automatically, even if nobody claims it?
questions.explanation: A player may claim a draw after 50 such moves, but since 2014 the arbiter must declare the game drawn after 75, unless the last move was checkmate.
questions.hintText: It is higher than the limit at which a player may claim the draw.

questions.question: A defender whose King has no legal move keeps offering his last Rook with check, because capturing it would be stalemate. What is such a Rook called?
questions.optionsString: A hanging rook|A passive rook|A pinned rook|A mad (rampant) rook
questions.explanation: The 'mad' or 'rampant' rook chases the enemy King with checks: if it is captured, the defender has no legal move left and the game is a stalemate draw.
questions.hintText: The Rook behaves as if it wanted to be captured at any price.
questions.acceptedAnswers: Mad rook|Rampant rook|Crazy rook|Desperado rook|Kamikaze rook

questions.question: The Vancura position is a drawing method for the defender in which endgame?
questions.optionsString: Rook and rook's pawn against rook|Queen and pawn against queen|Rook and bishop against rook|Bishop and pawn against knight
questions.explanation: In the Vancura position the defending Rook attacks the rook's pawn from the side (for example from f6 against a pawn on a6) and checks the King along the rank whenever it approaches.
questions.hintText: The defending piece attacks the pawn from the side and gives checks along the rank.

questions.question: In King and pawn versus King, a white pawn stands on e4. Which are its key squares, from which White's King forces promotion whoever is to move (unless the pawn is simply captured at once)?
questions.explanation: For a pawn that has not crossed the middle of the board, the key squares lie two ranks ahead of it on its own and the adjacent files: d6, e6 and f6.
questions.hintText: Standing directly in front of the pawn is not enough: the King must be further ahead.
questions.acceptedAnswers: d6 e6 f6|d6, e6 and f6

questions.question: White has a King on e5 and a pawn on e4; Black has a King on e7. No other pieces. What is the result with best play?
questions.optionsString: White wins whoever is to move|White wins only if White is to move|Draw whoever is to move|White wins only if Black is to move
questions.explanation: The Kings stand in opposition. If Black must move, White's King reaches a key square: 1... Kd7 2. Kf6. If White must move, Black keeps the opposition (1. Kd5 Kd7) and draws.
questions.hintText: The Kings face each other with one square between them: who is forced to give way?

questions.question: In rook and pawn versus rook, the defending King is driven off the queening square. To which side of the pawn should it go so that its Rook keeps enough checking distance?
questions.optionsString: The long side|Behind the pawn|The short side|It makes no difference
questions.explanation: The King goes to the short side so that the Rook can use the long side: there it has enough distance to keep checking from the flank without being attacked by the enemy King.
questions.hintText: The Rook needs as many files as possible between itself and the enemy King.

questions.question: For side checks to work in rook and pawn versus rook, at least how many empty files must lie between the defending Rook and the pawn?
questions.explanation: With three files between Rook and pawn, the attacking King cannot approach the Rook without abandoning the pawn. With less 'checking distance' the King attacks the Rook and the checks run out.
questions.hintText: The enemy King must not be able to reach the Rook and still protect its pawn.

questions.question: In rook versus bishop with no pawns, to which corner should the defending King head to hold the draw?
questions.optionsString: A corner of its bishop's colour|A corner of the opposite colour to its bishop|Any corner, it makes no difference|No corner: it must stay in the centre
questions.explanation: In the 'right' corner, of the opposite colour to the bishop, the bishop can block a Rook check next to its King and the attacker must release a stalemate. In the other corner the defender gets mated.
questions.hintText: The bishop must be able to shield its King on the square next to the corner.

questions.question: The Cochrane Defence is a standard drawing method in which pawnless endgame?
questions.optionsString: Queen against rook|Rook and knight against rook|Queen against two bishops|Rook and bishop against rook
questions.explanation: In rook and bishop against rook, the defending Rook pins the bishop against the attacking King, so the attacker cannot regroup. The ending is a theoretical draw but hard to hold in practice.
questions.hintText: The defending Rook pins a minor piece against the attacking King.

questions.question: The 'Troitsky line' belongs to the theory of which endgame?
questions.optionsString: Two knights against a pawn|Two bishops against a knight|Queen against a rook's pawn|Rook against two connected pawns
questions.explanation: Two knights cannot force mate against a lone King, but they can often win against King and pawn. Troitsky showed how far a pawn blockaded by a knight may have advanced for the win still to be forced.
questions.hintText: The line marks how far a blockaded pawn may have advanced for the stronger side to win.

questions.question: The Saavedra position (1895) is famous for which surprising winning move?
questions.optionsString: Promoting a pawn to a knight|Promoting a pawn to a bishop|Promoting a pawn to a rook|Sacrificing the new queen at once
questions.explanation: After 6. c8=Q? Rc4+! 7. Qxc4 Black is stalemated. Instead 6. c8=R! wins: the threat of Ra8+ forces 6... Ra4, and 7. Kb3 attacks the Rook while threatening Rc1 mate.
questions.hintText: Promoting to the strongest piece allows a stalemate trick, so a weaker piece is chosen.

questions.question: The pawn-endgame position known as the 'trébuchet' is the classic example of what?
questions.explanation: In the trébuchet each King attacks the enemy pawn and defends its own. Whoever is to move must abandon the pawn and loses, so both sides are in zugzwang.
questions.hintText: In this position neither player wants to be the one to move.

questions.question: The theory of 'corresponding squares' is used mainly to work out what?
questions.optionsString: Rook checks in rook endgames|Knight routes in closed positions|Queen checks in queen endgames|King manoeuvres in pawn endgames
questions.explanation: Each square of one King has a matching square for the other. The side that can always step onto the corresponding square avoids zugzwang; the opposition is the simplest case.
questions.hintText: The opposition is the simplest case of this theory.

questions.question: Lasker – Bauer, Amsterdam 1889, is the classic model of which combination?
questions.optionsString: The windmill|The smothered mate|The exchange sacrifice on c3|The double bishop sacrifice
questions.explanation: Lasker sacrificed both bishops, on h7 and then on g7, to strip the black King of its pawn cover; the Queen and a Rook finished the attack.
questions.hintText: Both sacrifices landed on the pawns in front of the castled King.

questions.question: Which game is known as the 'Immortal Zugzwang Game'?
questions.explanation: In Copenhagen 1923 Nimzowitsch, playing Black, tied Sämisch up so completely on a full board that every available move lost material, and White resigned.
questions.hintText: The winner wrote 'My System' and loved restraint and blockade.

questions.question: White has a Rook on a8 and a pawn on a7, with the King far away; Black's Rook stands behind the pawn on a1. On which kingside squares must Black's King stay to hold the draw?
questions.optionsString: e7 and f7|f6 and g6|g7 and h7|g8 and h8
questions.explanation: On g7 or h7 the King cannot be checked usefully. On f7 White wins with 1. Rh8! Rxa7 2. Rh7+, a skewer, and on the 6th rank a Rook check followed by a8=Q decides.
questions.hintText: Watch out for Rh8 followed by a check on the 7th rank, and for checks that free the a8 square.
questions.acceptedAnswers: h7 and g7|g7, h7|g7 h7|g7 or h7

questions.question: Rook plus f- and h-pawns against a lone Rook: what is the theoretical result of this ending in general, with correct defence?
questions.optionsString: A forced win in all normal positions|A win if the pawns are on the 5th rank|A win if the attacker has the move|A draw, although hard to defend
questions.explanation: Despite the two extra pawns, the standard positions with f- and h-pawns are drawn: the defender's King and Rook can stop both pawns from advancing safely. In practice the defence is hard, and many such endings have been lost.
questions.hintText: One file separates the pawns: they cannot protect each other and give their King little shelter.

questions.question: Two Kings face each other on the same file with no pieces between them. With how many empty squares between them does the side that is NOT to move hold the opposition?
questions.explanation: With an odd number of squares between the Kings (1, 3 or 5), the player who does not have to move holds the opposition: direct with one square, distant with three or five.
questions.hintText: Direct opposition is the closest case; the distant forms keep the same parity.

questions.question: A lone Queen faces a centre pawn on the 7th rank supported by its King; her own King is far away. How does she gain the time to bring her King closer?
questions.optionsString: By forcing the King in front of its own pawn|By pinning the pawn on the long diagonal|By giving checks only from the back rank|By sacrificing herself for the pawn
questions.explanation: The Queen approaches with checks and attacks on the pawn until the defending King must step onto the queening square to protect it. The blocked pawn cannot advance for one move, so the attacking King comes a step closer; then the process is repeated.
questions.hintText: The pawn cannot move while something stands on its queening square.

questions.question: In endings such as rook versus pawn, what is 'shouldering' (a body check)?
questions.optionsString: Using the King to block the enemy King's approach|Using the Rook to cut the King off along a rank|Pushing the pawn to deflect the enemy Rook|Checking from behind to drive the King forward
questions.explanation: The King steps into the path of the enemy King, so that it has to take a longer way round. That lost time often decides the race.
questions.hintText: Kings may never stand next to each other: one King can exploit that.

questions.question: In rook and pawn versus rook, against which pawns does the passive defence with the Rook on the back rank hold the draw?
questions.optionsString: Centre pawns only|Bishop's and centre pawns|Rook's and knight's pawns|All pawns alike
questions.explanation: Against a knight's or rook's pawn the attacker has no room to bring his Rook round to the far side of the defending King. Against bishop's and centre pawns that switch wins, so the defender needs an active defence there.
questions.hintText: The attacker wins by swinging his Rook to the other side of the King: when is there no room?
questions.acceptedAnswers: Knight's and rook's pawns|Knight and rook pawns|Rook and knight pawns

questions.question: In chess composition, what is the name for a sacrifice on the square where an enemy Rook's line and an enemy Bishop's line cross, so that whichever piece captures blocks the other?
questions.explanation: A Novotny is a sacrifice on the intersection of a Rook line and a Bishop line: each capture interferes with the other piece. Without the sacrifice the mutual interference is called a Grimshaw; with two like-moving pieces it is a Plachutta.
questions.hintText: It is named after the Czech composer who showed it in 1854.

questions.question: White has a King on d5 and a pawn on e6; Black has a King on e7 and is to move. No other pieces. Which move draws?
questions.explanation: The King must retreat straight back: 1... Ke8! 2. Kd6 Kd8 (opposition) 3. e7+ Ke8 4. Ke6 is stalemate. After 1... Kd8? 2. Kd6 Ke8 3. e7 or 1... Kf8? 2. Kd6 the pawn queens.
questions.hintText: Choose the retreat that lets you take the opposition whichever side White's King goes to.

questions.question: Under FIDE rules your flag falls. Your opponent has only a King and a knight; you have a King and a pawn. What is the result?
questions.optionsString: A draw, as a lone knight cannot mate|You lose, as a helpmate is still possible|A draw, as no mate can be forced|You lose only if the knight gives check
questions.explanation: On time, the game is drawn only if the opponent cannot checkmate by any series of legal moves. With your pawn on the board a mate is possible, for example when the pawn takes away your own King's flight square in a corner, so you lose.
questions.hintText: The test is not whether mate can be forced, but whether any legal sequence at all leads to mate.

packs.title: Quant Trader Speed Mental Math
packs.subtitle: High-speed probability, compound mental arithmetic & number theory
packs.author: Jane Street Prep Cohort

questions.question: Compute 35² (35 × 35) mentally.
questions.explanation: To square any number ending in 5: multiply the first digit n by (n+1), then append 25. 3 × 4 = 12 -> 1225.
questions.hintText: Squares of numbers ending in 5 have a shortcut: tens digit × the next digit up, then 25.

questions.question: Two fair 6-sided dice are rolled. How many of the 36 outcomes sum to exactly 7?
questions.explanation: The pairs summing to 7 are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) — exactly 6 outcomes.
questions.hintText: List the pairs in order, starting with a 1 on the first die.

questions.question: At an 8% annual compound return, approximately how many years does it take to double your portfolio?
questions.explanation: By the Rule of 72: Years to double ≈ 72 / Interest Rate = 72 / 8 = 9 years.
questions.hintText: Use the rule of 72.

questions.question: How many handshakes occur if 10 people in a room each shake hands with everyone else once?
questions.explanation: n(n - 1) / 2 = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 unique handshakes.
questions.hintText: Count each pair once: choose 2 people out of 10.

questions.question: What is 45² (45 × 45) calculated instantly?
questions.explanation: Rule for numbers ending in 5: 4 × (4 + 1) = 20, attach 25 -> 2025.
questions.hintText: Ends in 5? Multiply the tens digit by the next digit up, then put 25 on the end.

questions.question: What is 34 × 11 computed in your head?
questions.explanation: Insert sum of digits (3 + 4 = 7) between 3 and 4 -> 374.
questions.hintText: Multiplying by 11: add the two digits and write the sum between them.

questions.question: At an interest rate of 6% compounded annually, about how many years will it take for an investment to double?
questions.explanation: Rule of 72: Years = 72 / rate = 72 / 6 = 12 years.
questions.hintText: The rule of 72 gives a quick doubling time.

questions.question: What is 65² (65 × 65)?
questions.hintText: Use the ends-in-5 squaring trick: tens digit × the next digit, then 25.

questions.question: What is the probability of flipping two heads in two independent fair coin flips?
questions.hintText: Independent events: multiply their probabilities.

questions.question: What is 1200 / 25 calculated quickly?
questions.explanation: Dividing by 25 is multiplying by 4 and dividing by 100: (1200 × 4) / 100 = 4800 / 100 = 48.
questions.hintText: Think of 25 as a quarter of 100.

questions.question: What is 85² (85 × 85)?
questions.hintText: Squaring a number ending in 5: the tens digit times its successor, then 25 on the end.

questions.question: A game pays $10 with probability 0.5 and $0 with probability 0.5. What is the expected value E[X]?
questions.hintText: Weight each payout by its probability, then add.

questions.question: What is 103 × 105 computed mentally?
questions.hintText: Base-100 trick: cross-add the excess over 100, then multiply the two excesses.

questions.question: Flipping a fair coin until you see Heads. What is the EXPECTED number of flips required?
questions.explanation: For a geometric distribution with p = 0.5, expected trials E[N] = 1/p = 1/0.5 = 2 flips.
questions.hintText: The expected wait for a success is the reciprocal of its probability.

questions.question: What is 98 × 96 computed mentally?
questions.hintText: Base-100 trick: subtract one gap from the other number, then multiply the two gaps.

questions.question: What is the DELTA of a Call option that is deep in-the-money (almost certain to be exercised)?
questions.explanation: Deep in-the-money call options move dollar-for-dollar with the underlying asset, having a delta approaching +1.0.
questions.hintText: Delta is the change in the option's price per $1 move in the stock.

questions.question: What is 95² (95 × 95)?
questions.hintText: Ends-in-5 squares: tens digit times the next digit, followed by 25.

questions.question: If a bet has 60% win rate (p = 0.6) paying 1:1 (b = 1), what fraction f* of your bankroll should you bet according to Kelly (f = (bp - q) / b)?
questions.hintText: Remember q = 1 − p is the chance of losing.

questions.question: Which Greek measures the rate of decay of an option's price over time (time decay)?
questions.explanation: Theta represents the sensitivity of the option's value to the passage of time (daily decay).
questions.hintText: Options are wasting assets; this Greek is usually negative for an option you own.

questions.question: Disease affects 1% of population. Test has 90% true positive and 10% false positive. If a random person tests positive, what is the approximate probability they actually have the disease?
questions.hintText: Imagine 1000 people: how many true and how many false positives?

questions.question: The Sharpe Ratio of an investment portfolio is calculated as:
questions.optionsString: (Return - Benchmark) / Beta|(Return - Risk-Free Rate) / Volatility (σ)|Total Profit / Total Loss|Dividend Yield / Price
questions.explanation: Sharpe Ratio = (R_p - R_f) / σ_p, measuring risk-adjusted excess return per unit of volatility.
questions.hintText: Think 'reward per unit of risk', measured against a risk-free baseline.

questions.question: What is 125 × 32 computed mentally without a calculator?
questions.hintText: 125 is a neat fraction of 1000.

questions.question: In the Black-Scholes model, stock prices are assumed to follow which distribution?
questions.optionsString: Lognormal distribution (geometric Brownian motion)|Uniform distribution|Student's t-distribution with 1 degree of freedom|Binomial distribution
questions.explanation: Black-Scholes assumes underlying asset prices are lognormally distributed with constant volatility.
questions.hintText: Prices can't go negative, and they grow by percentages, not fixed amounts.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of people in a room required for the probability of at least two sharing a birthday to exceed 50%?
questions.explanation: With 23 people, there are C(23, 2) = 253 pairs; the probability of at least one shared birthday exceeds 50.7%.
questions.hintText: Count pairs of people, not people: pairs grow much faster than headcount.

questions.question: If an asset has an annual volatility of 16%, what is its daily volatility assuming 256 trading days in a year (Square Root of Time rule)?
questions.explanation: Daily σ = Annual σ / √256 = 16% / 16 = 1.0%.
questions.hintText: Volatility scales with the square root of time, not linearly.

questions.question: What is the number of distinct ways to choose 2 stocks from a universe of 20 stocks (C(20, 2))?
questions.hintText: A pair has no order: don't count A-then-B and B-then-A separately.

questions.question: What is the financial law stating that two assets with identical future cash flows must sell for the same price?
questions.optionsString: The Law of One Price|Fisher's Hypothesis|The Efficient Frontier|Pareto Optimality
questions.explanation: The Law of One Price states identical cash flows must have identical prices; otherwise, risk-free arbitrage exists.
questions.hintText: If prices differed, traders could profit with no risk.

questions.question: If customer orders arrive as a Poisson process at an average rate of λ = 3 per minute, what is the variance of the number of arrivals in one minute?
questions.explanation: In a Poisson distribution, the variance Var(X) is equal to the mean λ: Var(X) = λ = 3.
questions.hintText: Poisson counts have a famous link between variance and mean.

questions.question: What is 'slippage' in algorithmic execution?
questions.optionsString: A delay between the exchange and the trading server|The commission the broker charges for each order|The gap between an order's expected and actual fill price|A drift in the clock of the trading server hardware
questions.explanation: Slippage occurs during market volatility or latency when an order fills at a worse price than anticipated.
questions.hintText: Your order is sent at one price, but the market may move before it fills.

questions.question: If a stock falls by 50%, what percentage gain is required from the low to return to the original price?
questions.explanation: If a $100 stock drops to $50, it must gain $50 to reach $100 again. $50 / $50 = 100% gain required.
questions.hintText: Measure the gain against the new, smaller base, not the original price.

questions.question: What does Value at Risk (VaR) at 95% confidence for 1 day equal to $1,000,000 mean?
questions.optionsString: There is a 5% chance that the portfolio will lose more than $1,000,000 over the next day|The portfolio is guaranteed to make $1,000,000 in 95 days|The maximum loss possible is exactly $1,000,000|The portfolio has a 95% chance of zero loss
questions.explanation: 95% 1-day VaR means that in 95 out of 100 days losses will not exceed $1M (5% tail risk).
questions.hintText: Read it as a percentile of daily losses: how often are days worse than this?

questions.question: In the St. Petersburg game, the payout doubles on every coin flip (2, 4, 8, 16...). What is the theoretical expected value?
questions.explanation: Sum (1/2)^k × 2^k = 1 + 1 + 1 + ... = Infinity (St. Petersburg paradox).
questions.hintText: Write out probability × payout for the first few rounds and look at the pattern.

questions.question: For European options on non-dividend stock, what fundamental relationship links Call (C) and Put (P) with Strike K and Stock S?
questions.optionsString: C + P = S + K × e^(-rT)|C - P = S - K × e^(-rT)|C - P = S + K × e^(-rT)|C × P = S × K × e^(-rT)
questions.explanation: Put-Call Parity: C - P = S - K × e^(-rT) (or C + K×e^(-rT) = P + S).
questions.hintText: Two portfolios with identical payoffs at expiry must cost the same today.

questions.question: What is 15% of 240?
questions.explanation: 10% of 240 is 24 and 5% is half of that, 12. Together: 24 + 12 = 36.
questions.hintText: Split it into 10% plus 5%.

questions.question: What is 7/8 written as a decimal?
questions.hintText: Start from 1/8 and subtract it from 1.

questions.question: A stock rises from $80 to $100. What is the percentage gain?
questions.explanation: The gain is $20 on a base of $80: 20 / 80 = 0.25 = 25%. Dividing by 100 instead gives the tempting 20%.
questions.hintText: Divide the gain by the starting price, not the final price.

questions.question: What is 36 × 25, worked out in your head?
questions.hintText: Multiplying by 25 is dividing by 4 and adding two zeros.

questions.question: What is 3/20 written as a percentage?
questions.explanation: Scale the fraction to hundredths: 3/20 = 15/100 = 15%.
questions.hintText: Multiply top and bottom by 5 to get a denominator of 100.

questions.question: You draw one card from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is an ace?
questions.explanation: There are 4 aces among 52 cards: 4/52 = 1/13.
questions.hintText: Count the aces in the deck, then simplify the fraction.

questions.question: What is 99 × 47, worked out in your head?
questions.hintText: Multiply by 100 first, then take one 47 away.

questions.question: What is 2 to the power of 10?
questions.explanation: Doubling ten times: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024. It is close to 1000, which makes it a handy benchmark.
questions.hintText: 2 to the power of 5 is 32; square that.

questions.question: What is the mean of 12, 15, 18, 23 and 32?
questions.hintText: Add the five numbers, then divide by how many there are.

questions.question: What is the median of 7, 3, 12, 9 and 4?
questions.explanation: Sorted, the numbers are 3, 4, 7, 9, 12. The middle one is 7; 12 is only the middle of the unsorted list.
questions.hintText: Sort the numbers first, then take the middle one.

questions.question: You invest $2,000 at 5% simple interest per year. How much interest do you earn in 3 years?
questions.explanation: Simple interest is paid on the original amount only: 2,000 × 0.05 = $100 a year, so $300 in 3 years. About $315 would be the compound result.
questions.hintText: Simple interest: the same amount is added every year.

questions.question: A profit of $600 is split between two partners in the ratio 2:3. How much does the partner with the larger share get?
questions.explanation: 2 + 3 = 5 parts, so one part is 600 / 5 = $120. The larger share is 3 parts: 3 × 120 = $360.
questions.hintText: Add the ratio numbers to find how many equal parts there are.

questions.question: Interest rates are often quoted in basis points, where 1 basis point is 0.01%. How many basis points is 0.25%?
questions.explanation: 0.25% / 0.01% = 25 basis points. A full 1% is 100 basis points.
questions.hintText: Divide the percentage by the size of one basis point.

questions.question: What is 12.5% of 640?
questions.explanation: 12.5% is exactly 1/8, and 640 / 8 = 80.
questions.hintText: 12.5% is a simple unit fraction; divide instead of multiplying.

questions.question: What is the expected value of one roll of a fair six-sided die?
questions.explanation: Each face has probability 1/6: (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 21 / 6 = 3.5. The expected value need not be a face you can actually roll.
questions.hintText: Average the six faces.

questions.question: What is 3/5 + 1/4 written as a decimal?
questions.hintText: Turn each fraction into a decimal first.

questions.question: What is the square root of 196?
questions.explanation: 14 × 14 = 196. A quick check: the root must end in 4 or 6 because the square ends in 6, and 16 × 16 = 256 is too big.
questions.hintText: The square ends in 6, so the root ends in 4 or 6.

questions.question: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of a number greater than 4?
questions.explanation: Only 5 and 6 are greater than 4: 2 of 6 outcomes, 2/6 = 1/3.
questions.hintText: List the faces that qualify; 'greater than' excludes 4 itself.

questions.question: 54 is what percentage of 180?
questions.hintText: Find 10% of 180 first, then see how many times it fits.

questions.question: What is 1/6 as a decimal, rounded to three decimal places?
questions.explanation: 1/6 = 0.1666..., which rounds to 0.167. For comparison, 1/7 ≈ 0.143 and 1/8 = 0.125.
questions.hintText: It is half of 1/3.

questions.question: What is 435 ÷ 5, worked out in your head?
questions.explanation: Dividing by 5 is doubling and then dividing by 10: 435 × 2 = 870, and 870 / 10 = 87.
questions.hintText: Double the number, then move the decimal point one place.

questions.question: A fair coin is flipped 5 times. How many different sequences of heads and tails are possible?
questions.explanation: Each flip has 2 outcomes, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32 sequences. 10 would be 5 × 2, which adds instead of multiplying.
questions.hintText: Each flip multiplies the number of sequences by two.

questions.question: A share costs $50 and pays a dividend of $2 per year. What is its dividend yield?
questions.explanation: Dividend yield = annual dividend / price = 2 / 50 = 0.04 = 4%. 25% comes from dividing the wrong way round.
questions.hintText: Divide the yearly dividend by the share price.

questions.question: A share price rises by 10% and then falls by 10%. How does the final price compare with the starting price?
questions.explanation: 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, so the price ends 1% lower. The fall is taken from a larger base than the rise.
questions.hintText: Multiply the two growth factors instead of adding the percentages.

questions.question: An investment doubles in about 6 years. Roughly what annual compound return does that imply?
questions.explanation: Rule of 72 in reverse: rate ≈ 72 / years = 72 / 6 = 12%. The exact figure is about 12.2%.
questions.hintText: Turn the rule of 72 around: divide by the years instead of the rate.

questions.question: You invest $10,000 at 10% per year, compounded annually. How much do you have after 3 years?
questions.explanation: Multiply by 1.1 three times: 10,000 → 11,000 → 12,100 → 13,310. $13,000 would be simple interest.
questions.hintText: Multiply by 1.1 once per year; do not just add 10% three times.

questions.question: You roll a fair die and win as many dollars as the number shown, except that a 6 pays nothing. What is the expected payout?
questions.explanation: The payouts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 0 are equally likely: (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 0) / 6 = 15 / 6 = $2.50.
questions.hintText: Add the six possible payouts, counting the zero, and divide by 6.

questions.question: What is the sum of the infinite series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ...?
questions.explanation: Each term halves the remaining gap to 2: 1, 1.5, 1.75, 1.875, ... The formula a / (1 − r) with a = 1 and r = 1/2 gives 1 / (1/2) = 2.
questions.hintText: Use a / (1 − r) for a geometric series whose ratio r is below 1.

questions.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is at least 10?
questions.hintText: Count the outcomes for each qualifying sum separately, then add.

questions.question: You draw one card from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is a heart or a king?
questions.explanation: 13 hearts + 4 kings − 1 king of hearts counted twice = 16 cards. 16/52 = 4/13.
questions.hintText: One card is both a heart and a king; do not count it twice.

questions.question: How many different 3-person committees can be chosen from 8 people?
questions.explanation: Order does not matter: C(8, 3) = (8 × 7 × 6) / (3 × 2 × 1) = 336 / 6 = 56. 336 counts every committee 6 times, once per ordering.
questions.hintText: Count ordered picks first, then divide by the orderings of three people.

questions.question: What is 76 × 74, worked out in your head?
questions.explanation: Same tens digit and units adding to 10: 7 × 8 = 56, then 6 × 4 = 24, giving 5624. Check: 75² − 1² = 5625 − 1.
questions.hintText: Same tens digit, units adding to ten: tens digit × the next digit, then the units product.

questions.question: Quarterly revenue grows from $250 million to $400 million. What is the percentage increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is 150 on a base of 250: 150 / 250 = 0.6 = 60%. 37.5% divides by the new value instead of the old one.
questions.hintText: Divide the increase by the earlier figure.

questions.question: What is the square root of 50, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 7² = 49 is just below 50. The missing 1, divided by 2 × 7 = 14, adds about 0.07, so √50 ≈ 7.07, which rounds to 7.1.
questions.hintText: Start from the nearest perfect square and add a small correction.

questions.question: A portfolio has 60% in a fund that returns 10% and 40% in a fund that returns 5%. What is the portfolio's return?
questions.explanation: Weight each return: 0.6 × 10% + 0.4 × 5% = 6% + 2% = 8%. The plain average, 7.5%, ignores the weights.
questions.hintText: Multiply each return by its weight, then add.

questions.question: How fast is 72 km/h in metres per second?
questions.explanation: Divide by 3.6, because 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h: 72 / 3.6 = 20 m/s. In full: 72,000 m in 3,600 s.
questions.hintText: One hour has 3,600 seconds and one kilometre has 1,000 metres.

questions.question: A bet wins $3 with probability p and loses $1 otherwise. For which value of p is the bet exactly fair (expected value zero)?
questions.explanation: Set the expected value to zero: 3p − 1 × (1 − p) = 0, so 4p = 1 and p = 25%. A payout of 3 to 1 needs a win one time in four.
questions.hintText: Write the expected value as winnings minus losses and set it to zero.

questions.question: A portfolio holds stocks and bonds in the ratio 7:3. The bonds are worth $45,000. What is the whole portfolio worth?
questions.explanation: Bonds are 3 parts, so one part is 45,000 / 3 = $15,000. The portfolio has 7 + 3 = 10 parts: 10 × 15,000 = $150,000. $105,000 is the stocks alone.
questions.hintText: Find the value of one part from the bonds, then count all the parts.

questions.question: What is 3.6 ÷ 0.04?
questions.explanation: Multiply both numbers by 100 to clear the decimals: 360 ÷ 4 = 90.
questions.hintText: Scale both numbers by the same power of ten until the divisor is whole.

questions.question: You invest $1,000 at 10% per year for 2 years. How much more do you earn with annual compounding than with simple interest?
questions.explanation: Simple interest pays 100 + 100 = $200. Compounding pays 100 + 110 = $210, because the second year also earns 10% on the first year's $100. The difference is $10.
questions.hintText: The only extra is the interest earned on the first year's interest.

questions.question: The average of five numbers is 12. A sixth number is added and the average rises to 13. What is the sixth number?
questions.explanation: Five numbers sum to 5 × 12 = 60; six numbers must sum to 6 × 13 = 78. The new number is 78 − 60 = 18.
questions.hintText: Work with totals: average times count, before and after.

questions.question: You drive 60 km at 30 km/h and then drive the same 60 km back at 60 km/h. What is your average speed for the whole trip?
questions.explanation: Average speed is total distance over total time: 120 km in 2 h + 1 h = 3 h, which is 40 km/h. 45 km/h averages the two speeds and ignores that the slow leg takes longer.
questions.hintText: Work out the total time first; do not average the two speeds.

questions.question: What is 37 × 27, worked out in your head?
questions.hintText: 37 × 3 gives a number with three equal digits.

questions.question: A resting heart beats about 70 times per minute. About how many times does it beat in one day?
questions.explanation: A day has 24 × 60 = 1,440 minutes, and 70 × 1,440 = 100,800, so about 100,000 beats.
questions.hintText: First count the minutes in a day.

questions.question: A fair coin is flipped 4 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
questions.explanation: There are C(4, 2) = 6 ways to place the 2 heads among 16 equally likely sequences: 6/16 = 3/8. One half is tempting, but 2 heads is only the most likely count, not a sure thing.
questions.hintText: Count the sequences with two heads, then divide by all sequences.

questions.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that at least one of them shows a 6?
questions.explanation: Use the complement: P(no 6) = 5/6 × 5/6 = 25/36, so P(at least one 6) = 11/36. Adding 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3 counts the double six twice.
questions.hintText: Find the chance that neither die shows a 6, then subtract from 1.

questions.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the expected value of the larger of the two numbers, to two decimal places?
questions.hintText: Count how many of the 36 outcomes have each value as the maximum.

questions.question: You roll a fair die and may either take the number shown in dollars or roll once more and take the second result instead. With the best strategy, what is the game's expected value?
questions.explanation: A second roll is worth $3.50 on average, so keep a 4, 5 or 6 and re-roll a 1, 2 or 3. E = 1/2 × 5 + 1/2 × 3.5 = 2.5 + 1.75 = $4.25.
questions.hintText: Compare the first roll with the average value of one more roll.

questions.question: Money grows at 9% per year, compounded annually. By roughly what factor does it grow in 24 years?
questions.explanation: By the rule of 72, money doubles about every 72 / 9 = 8 years. In 24 years it doubles 3 times: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 (exactly 7.9). About 3 times would be simple interest.
questions.hintText: Find the doubling time first, then count the doublings.

questions.question: A fund gains 21% in total over two years. What constant annual compound return gives the same result?
questions.explanation: You need (1 + r)² = 1.21. Since 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21, r = 10%. Halving 21% gives 10.5%, which forgets that the second year also earns a return on the first year's gain.
questions.hintText: Look for the growth factor whose square is 1.21.

questions.question: What is 997 × 1003, worked out in your head?
questions.hintText: Both numbers are the same distance from 1000: use a² − b².

questions.question: What is the cube root of 2197?
questions.explanation: 10³ = 1000 and 20³ = 8000, so the root is between 10 and 20. A cube ending in 7 needs a root ending in 3 (3³ = 27), so it is 13: 13 × 13 × 13 = 169 × 13 = 2197.
questions.hintText: Bracket it between 10³ and 20³, then look at the last digit.

questions.question: Three fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that all three show the same number?
questions.explanation: The first die can be anything; each of the other two must match it with probability 1/6: 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36. 1/216 is the chance of one specific triple, such as three sixes.
questions.hintText: Let the first die land freely; what must the other two do?

questions.question: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that they are of the same suit?
questions.explanation: Whatever the first card is, 12 of the remaining 51 cards share its suit: 12/51 = 4/17, a little under 1/4.
questions.hintText: Fix the first card, then count the matching cards still in the deck.

questions.question: In how many different ways can 6 people sit around a round table if rotations of the same arrangement count as one?
questions.explanation: Seat one person anywhere to fix the rotation, then arrange the other five: 5! = 120. 720 = 6! would count each arrangement 6 times.
questions.hintText: Fix one person's seat, then arrange everyone else.

questions.question: On a street grid you must travel 4 blocks east and 4 blocks north. How many different shortest routes are there?
questions.explanation: Every shortest route is a sequence of 8 moves, 4 of them east. Choosing which 4 are east gives C(8, 4) = (8 × 7 × 6 × 5) / (4 × 3 × 2 × 1) = 1680 / 24 = 70.
questions.hintText: A route is a sequence of 8 moves; choose which of them go east.

questions.question: You draw one card from a standard 52-card deck. An ace pays $10, a jack, queen or king pays $5, and any other card pays nothing. What is the fair price of the game, to the nearest cent?
questions.explanation: There are 4 aces and 12 face cards: E = (4 × 10 + 12 × 5) / 52 = 100 / 52 ≈ $1.92.
questions.hintText: Add up the payouts over all 52 cards, then divide by 52.

questions.question: A family has two children, and you are told that at least one of them is a boy. Assuming boys and girls are equally likely and independent, what is the probability that both are boys?
questions.explanation: The equally likely cases are BB, BG, GB and GG. 'At least one boy' rules out GG, leaving three cases, of which only BB has two boys: 1/3.
questions.hintText: List all four birth orders, then cross out the ones the clue excludes.

questions.question: At a continuously compounded rate of 7% per year, about how long does money take to double? (ln 2 ≈ 0.693)
questions.hintText: Set e^(rt) equal to 2 and take the natural logarithm of both sides.

questions.question: What is the present value of $1,210 received in 2 years if the discount rate is 10% per year, compounded annually?
questions.explanation: Discount once per year: 1,210 / 1.1 = 1,100, and 1,100 / 1.1 = 1,000. So PV = 1,210 / 1.21 = $1,000. $1,100 discounts only one year.
questions.hintText: Divide by the growth factor once for each year.

questions.question: A perpetuity pays $50 at the end of every year, forever. At a discount rate of 4% per year, what is it worth today?
questions.explanation: The present value of a perpetuity is payment / rate: 50 / 0.04 = $1,250. Check: $1,250 invested at 4% yields exactly $50 a year.
questions.hintText: Which sum, invested at this rate, would pay out the same amount every year?

questions.question: How many digits does the number 2 to the power of 100 have when written out in full?
questions.explanation: log₁₀ 2 ≈ 0.301, so 2^100 ≈ 10^30.1. A number between 10^30 and 10^31 has 31 digits. Equivalently, 2^10 ≈ 10^3 gives 2^100 ≈ 1.27 × 10^30.
questions.hintText: The base-ten logarithm of 2 is about 0.301.

questions.question: Two uncorrelated positions have daily volatilities of $3 million and $4 million. What is the volatility of the combined position?
questions.explanation: For uncorrelated positions the variances add: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, and √25 = 5. Volatilities only add up to $7 million when the positions move perfectly together.
questions.hintText: Variances add for uncorrelated positions; volatilities do not.

questions.question: How many zeros are at the end of 25! (25 factorial)?
questions.explanation: Each trailing zero needs a factor 2 × 5, and fives are the scarce ones. The multiples of 5 up to 25 give five fives (5, 10, 15, 20, 25), and 25 = 5 × 5 gives one more: 6 zeros.
questions.hintText: Count the factors of 5, and remember that some numbers contain more than one.

questions.question: How many positive divisors does 360 have?
questions.explanation: Factorise: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. A divisor picks an exponent 0–3 for 2, 0–2 for 3 and 0–1 for 5: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 divisors.
questions.hintText: Write the prime factorisation, add 1 to each exponent, then multiply.

questions.question: You are dealt 13 cards from a standard 52-card deck. What is the expected number of aces in your hand?
questions.explanation: Each of the 4 aces lands in your hand with probability 13/52 = 1/4. By linearity of expectation, the expected count is 4 × 1/4 = 1.
questions.hintText: Find the chance that one particular ace is in your hand, then add over all aces.

questions.question: A prize is behind one of three doors. You pick a door; the host, who knows where the prize is, always opens one of the other two doors that is empty and offers you a switch. What is your chance of winning if you switch?
questions.explanation: Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time. In the other 2/3 of cases the host's reveal leaves the prize behind the remaining door, so switching wins with probability 2/3.
questions.hintText: How often was your first pick wrong? Switching wins in exactly those cases.

packs.title: Astrophysics & Relativistic Mechanics
packs.subtitle: Escape velocity, orbital resonances, thermodynamics & photon energy
packs.author: CERN Open Curricula

questions.question: Approximately how many minutes does it take sunlight to travel 1 AU from the Sun to Earth?
questions.explanation: At c ≈ 300,000 km/s across 150 million km, light takes ~500 seconds ≈ 8.3 minutes.
questions.hintText: Time = distance ÷ speed; light covers about 300,000 km every second.

questions.question: If the distance between two masses is tripled (3r), by what factor does their gravitational attraction decrease (1/N)? Enter N:
questions.explanation: Newton's Universal Gravitation follows an inverse-square law (1/r²). Tripling r reduces force by 3² = 9.
questions.hintText: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: F ∝ 1/r².

questions.question: Earth's escape velocity is approximately how many km/s (rounded to the nearest integer)?
questions.explanation: v_escape = sqrt(2GM/R) ≈ 11.2 km/s (rounded to 11 km/s).
questions.hintText: Escape speed is √2 times the circular-orbit speed near the surface.

questions.question: What optical shift in light spectra proved to Edwin Hubble that distant galaxies are moving away from us?
questions.explanation: Light from receding galaxies is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths (redshift) as space expands; farther galaxies show a bigger shift.
questions.hintText: Think of a siren dropping in pitch as the ambulance drives away: the same effect for light.

questions.question: According to Planck's relation, the energy of a photon is directly proportional to its:
questions.explanation: Planck's equation states that photon energy E equals Planck's constant h multiplied by its frequency f.
questions.hintText: Compare the energy of a gamma-ray photon with that of a radio photon.

questions.question: What is the Chandrasekhar limit (~1.4 solar masses)?
questions.optionsString: The minimum mass a gas cloud needs to ignite hydrogen fusion|The maximum mass a white dwarf can have and stay stable|The maximum mass of a neutron star before it collapses further|The upper mass limit of stars on the main sequence
questions.explanation: Above ~1.4 solar masses, electron degeneracy pressure cannot prevent gravitational collapse in a white dwarf.
questions.hintText: It marks where electron degeneracy pressure stops holding a stellar remnant up.

questions.question: In General Relativity, how does time pass near a massive body (like a neutron star or black hole) compared to deep empty space?
questions.optionsString: Time passes SLOWER near the massive object|Time passes FASTER near the massive object|Time flows in reverse|Time is completely unaffected by gravity
questions.explanation: Stronger gravitational potential slows down proper time relative to a distant observer (gravitational time dilation).
questions.hintText: Think of GPS: satellite clocks need correcting because gravity is weaker up there.

questions.question: What is the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation with temperature ~2.725 Kelvin?
questions.optionsString: Microwaves emitted by microwave ovens|Thermal radiation released ~380,000 years after the Big Bang|Light from nearby stars reflecting off asteroid dust|Signals from communication satellites
questions.explanation: The CMB is ancient relic radiation from the recombination era when the universe first became transparent to light.
questions.hintText: It reaches us evenly from every direction in the sky, not from any single source.

questions.question: What is the Schwarzschild radius of a non-rotating mass M (formula for the event horizon radius)?
questions.optionsString: r_s = GM / c²|r_s = 2GM / c²|r_s = GM / 2c²|r_s = √(2GM / c)
questions.explanation: The Schwarzschild radius is r_s = 2GM / c², setting escape velocity equal to the speed of light c.
questions.hintText: Derived from ½mv² = GMm/r when v = c.

questions.question: For which breakthrough discovery did Albert Einstein win the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921?
questions.optionsString: Special Relativity (E = mc²)|General Relativity (Curved spacetime)|Explanation of the Photoelectric Effect using light quanta (photons)|Bose-Einstein Condensation
questions.explanation: Einstein was awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize for his law of the photoelectric effect, establishing the quantum nature of light.
questions.hintText: The committee did not cite either of his relativity theories.

questions.question: How do atomic nuclei fuse inside the Sun despite their mutual electrostatic Coulomb repulsion?
questions.optionsString: Quantum tunneling through the Coulomb barrier|The Sun has a gigantic mechanical compressor|Protons lose their electric charge at 10 million Kelvin|Magnetic field eliminates all electric repulsion
questions.explanation: The core of the Sun (~15M K) is not hot enough for classical fusion; quantum tunneling allows protons to overcome the Coulomb barrier.
questions.hintText: Classically the protons are too slow; think of what wave-like particles can do at a barrier.

questions.question: What did Albert Einstein famously call quantum entanglement due to its non-local correlation across space?
questions.optionsString: Cosmic harmony|Spooky action at a distance|The holographic mirror|Wavefunction hallucination
questions.explanation: Einstein was uncomfortable with instantaneous non-local state collapse and called it 'spooky action at a distance'.
questions.hintText: He objected that it seemed to need instant influence across distance.

questions.question: What relates the wavelength λ of any matter particle to its linear momentum p (p = m·v)?
questions.optionsString: λ = p / h|λ = h·p|λ = h / p|λ = p² / 2m
questions.explanation: De Broglie's matter wave equation states λ = h / p, where h is Planck's constant and p is momentum.
questions.hintText: Check units: h is in J·s, p in kg·m/s, and λ must come out as a length.

questions.question: What is the theoretical radiation that black holes are predicted to emit due to quantum vacuum fluctuations near the event horizon?
questions.explanation: Stephen Hawking showed in 1974 that quantum particle-antiparticle pairs near the horizon cause black holes to slowly radiate and evaporate.
questions.hintText: A 1974 prediction linking quantum theory, gravity and heat; named after its author.

questions.question: What do experimental violations of Bell's inequalities definitively prove about our universe?
questions.optionsString: The universe cannot be both local and realistic|The speed of light can be exceeded by spaceships|Electrons do not possess spin|Gravity does not exist at micro-scales
questions.explanation: Bell proved that local hidden-variable theories must obey an inequality; experiments (Clauser, Aspect, Zeilinger) violate it, so nature cannot be both local and realistic.
questions.hintText: Ask which of Einstein's assumptions about particles in the EPR argument the experiments undermine.

questions.question: As a particle with mass approaches the speed of light (v -> c), what happens to its relativistic momentum and energy?
questions.optionsString: They remain constant|They drop to zero|They grow without limit, approaching infinity|They turn negative
questions.explanation: The Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 - v²/c²) diverges to infinity as v approaches c, preventing any mass from reaching c.
questions.hintText: Look at γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) as v gets close to c.

questions.question: What outward quantum pressure halts the gravitational collapse in a neutron star?
questions.optionsString: Thermal gas pressure|Neutron degeneracy pressure|Electron repulsion|Electromagnetic radiation pressure
questions.explanation: Neutron degeneracy pressure, governed by the Pauli Exclusion Principle for fermions, supports the neutron star against gravity.
questions.hintText: A purely quantum effect: it would persist even if the star cooled to absolute zero.

questions.question: How does Einstein's theory of gravity describe the gravitational orbit of Earth around the Sun?
questions.optionsString: Earth follows a geodesic in spacetime curved by the Sun's mass|An invisible magnetic tether pulls Earth|Subatomic gravitons physically push Earth like wind|Earth is suspended in liquid ether
questions.explanation: Mass tells spacetime how to curve; spacetime tells mass how to move along geodesics.
questions.hintText: In general relativity gravity is geometry, not a pulling force: Earth moves freely.

questions.question: What percentage of the total mass-energy budget of the observable universe is estimated to consist of Dark Energy?
questions.explanation: Dark Energy constitutes ~68%, Dark Matter ~27%, and ordinary baryonic matter is only about 5%.
questions.hintText: Ordinary matter, dark matter and dark energy must add up to 100%.

questions.question: What is the spin quantum number of all fermions (such as electrons, quarks, protons, and neutrons)?
questions.explanation: Fermions obey Fermi-Dirac statistics and possess half-integer spin (electrons have spin 1/2). Bosons have integer spin.
questions.hintText: Take the electron's spin and generalise; bosons such as the photon have spin 1.

questions.question: What is the heaviest chemical element that can be produced in the core of a massive star via exothermic nuclear fusion before it collapses into a supernova?
questions.explanation: Nuclei around iron and nickel have the highest binding energy per nucleon, so fusing iron absorbs energy rather than releasing it. With no energy source left, the core collapses under gravity.
questions.hintText: Fusion stops paying off at the peak of the binding-energy curve.

questions.question: A spaceship flies toward you at half the speed of light and switches on its headlights. What speed do you measure for that light?
questions.optionsString: Half of c|Exactly c|1.5 times c|Twice c
questions.explanation: Einstein's second postulate says that light in a vacuum moves at c for every observer, whatever the motion of its source. The ship's speed is not added to it; it only shifts the light toward the blue.
questions.hintText: Recall Einstein's second postulate about light and moving sources.
questions.acceptedAnswers: c|the speed of light|speed of light

questions.question: What happens when light from a distant quasar passes close to a massive galaxy cluster?
questions.optionsString: The light slows down to a complete halt|The light's path bends, giving magnified or multiple images|The light is converted into radio waves|The light turns into dark matter
questions.explanation: Gravitational lensing acts as a cosmic magnifying glass, bending photon trajectories around massive spacetime distortions.
questions.hintText: In general relativity light follows the geometry of spacetime; massive objects change that geometry.

questions.question: What does the Second Law of Thermodynamics imply about the ultimate fate of the universe in the 'Heat Death' scenario?
questions.optionsString: Entropy will decrease to zero|Entropy will reach a maximum, leaving no usable energy|All stars will re-ignite simultaneously|The temperature will reach infinity
questions.explanation: At maximum cosmic entropy, all energy is evenly distributed at uniform temperature, ending all thermodynamic work.
questions.hintText: Entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease; where does it end up in the long run?

questions.question: In the Schrödinger's Cat thought experiment, what causes the cat's state to resolve from a superposition to a definite outcome in the Copenhagen interpretation?
questions.optionsString: Decoherence by heat|The passage of 1 hour|The act of measurement (wavefunction collapse)|Nuclear decay
questions.explanation: In the Copenhagen interpretation, physical measurement collapses the wave function |ψ⟩ into an eigenstate.
questions.hintText: In the Copenhagen view the state stays undefined until a particular kind of act is done to it.

questions.question: What does Hubble's Constant H₀ measure?
questions.optionsString: The expansion rate of the universe (~70 km/s per Mpc)|The total mass of the Milky Way|The temperature of the sun's corona|The speed of gravitational waves
questions.explanation: Hubble's constant relates recession velocity to distance: v = H₀ × d, measuring cosmic expansion.
questions.hintText: Hubble's law is v = H₀·d: think about what v and d stand for.
questions.acceptedAnswers: Expansion rate|Expansion rate of the universe

questions.question: What fundamental property does the Higgs field impart to elementary particles (like quarks and W/Z bosons) through their interaction with it?
questions.optionsString: Electric charge|Rest mass|Color charge|Magnetic dipole moment
questions.explanation: Particles gain inertial mass through the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism by interacting with the non-zero vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field.
questions.hintText: Compare the W and Z bosons, which feel this field, with the photon, which does not.

questions.question: What minute anomaly in Mercury's orbit could NOT be explained by Newtonian gravity, but was precisely predicted by Einstein's General Relativity?
questions.optionsString: Its orbital period was slowing down|Perihelion precession of 43 arcseconds per century|Its orbit was becoming more circular|Its axial tilt was changing
questions.explanation: The curvature of spacetime near the Sun accounts for the extra 43 arcseconds per century in Mercury's perihelion shift.
questions.hintText: It concerns Mercury's elliptical orbit and how it slowly shifts over centuries.
questions.acceptedAnswers: Perihelion precession|Precession of the perihelion|Perihelion shift

questions.question: Gravitational waves, directly detected by LIGO in 2015 from colliding black holes, propagate through space at what speed?
questions.optionsString: The speed of light in vacuum (c)|Infinite speed|Speed of sound|Half the speed of light
questions.explanation: In General Relativity, ripples in the curvature of spacetime propagate at exactly the speed of light c.
questions.hintText: A 2017 neutron-star merger was seen in gravitational waves and gamma rays: compare arrival times.
questions.acceptedAnswers: Speed of light|The speed of light|Light speed

questions.question: What virtual force-carrier particle mediates the electromagnetic force between charged particles in QED?
questions.explanation: In quantum electrodynamics (QED), electromagnetic interactions occur through the exchange of virtual photons.
questions.hintText: In QED the carrier is the quantum of the electromagnetic field itself: what do lamps emit?

questions.question: What is the fundamental physical significance of the Planck Length (~1.616 × 10⁻³⁵ meters)?
questions.optionsString: The size of a hydrogen atom|The diameter of a quark|The scale where quantum gravity effects dominate|The wavelength of visible light
questions.explanation: Below the Planck scale, quantum fluctuations of spacetime geometry become so severe that smooth manifolds cease to exist.
questions.hintText: It is built from just three constants: G, ħ and c.

questions.question: What bizarre macroscopic quantum state occurs when bosons are cooled to temperatures within nanokelvins of absolute zero?
questions.optionsString: They vaporize explosively|Atoms occupy one ground state and act as a single wave|They turn into antimatter|Their mass becomes infinite
questions.explanation: In a BEC, millions of bosons lose individual identity and merge into a coherent macroscopic quantum super-atom.
questions.hintText: Bosons may all share one quantum state: what happens when they all do?

questions.question: What fundamental quantum rule dictates that no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state simultaneously?
questions.optionsString: Heisenberg's matrix|The Pauli Exclusion Principle|Fermi's golden rule|Newton's 3rd law
questions.explanation: Wolfgang Pauli showed that multi-fermion wavefunctions must be anti-symmetric under particle exchange, giving matter stability and volume.
questions.hintText: It explains why electrons fill atomic shells instead of all sitting in the lowest level.

questions.question: According to Kepler's first law, what shape is a planet's orbit around the Sun?
questions.optionsString: A circle with the Sun at its centre|An ellipse with the Sun at one focus|An ellipse with the Sun at its centre|A parabola with the Sun at its focus
questions.explanation: Kepler found that planets move on ellipses, with the Sun at one of the two focal points and not in the middle. A circle is only the special case of an ellipse with zero eccentricity.
questions.hintText: A planet is sometimes nearer to the Sun and sometimes farther: which curve allows that?

questions.question: What does Einstein's equation E = mc² express?
questions.optionsString: Mass and energy are equivalent|Energy grows with the square of speed|Mass increases with temperature|Light has a small rest mass
questions.explanation: E = mc² says that a mass m corresponds to an energy of m times the speed of light squared. Because c² is huge, a tiny amount of mass equals an enormous amount of energy.
questions.hintText: Here c is a fixed constant, so the equation links just two quantities.

questions.question: A clock flies past you at 90% of the speed of light. Compared with your own clock, how do you see it tick?
questions.explanation: This is time dilation: a clock moving relative to you runs slow by the Lorentz factor γ. At 90% of light speed γ is about 2.3, so the moving clock ticks less than half as fast.
questions.hintText: Special relativity calls this effect time dilation: moving clocks are affected.

questions.question: Which process powers a main-sequence star such as the Sun?
questions.optionsString: Fission of uranium nuclei|Chemical burning of hydrogen|Fusion of helium into carbon|Fusion of hydrogen into helium
questions.explanation: A main-sequence star fuses hydrogen nuclei into helium in its core, and the lost mass is released as energy. Helium fusion into carbon only starts later, in the red-giant phase.
questions.hintText: Think of the lightest element, which makes up most of a young star.

questions.question: What kind of remnant will the Sun leave behind after its red-giant phase?
questions.explanation: The Sun is far too light to explode as a supernova. It will shed its outer layers as a planetary nebula, and its hot carbon–oxygen core will remain as a white dwarf.
questions.hintText: Only stars above about 8 solar masses end in a supernova; the Sun ends more quietly.

questions.question: What is the event horizon of a black hole?
questions.optionsString: The point at the centre with infinite density|The bright disc of hot gas orbiting the hole|The boundary from inside which no light can escape|The region where time starts to run backwards
questions.explanation: The event horizon is the surface of no return: inside it, the escape speed exceeds the speed of light, so nothing can get out. The central point is called the singularity, and the glowing gas is the accretion disc.
questions.hintText: A horizon is a limit beyond which you cannot see events.

questions.question: Which star colour indicates the highest surface temperature?
questions.explanation: By Wien's law, a hotter body radiates most strongly at a shorter wavelength. The hottest stars (above about 10,000 K) therefore look blue, while cool stars of about 3,000 K look red.
questions.hintText: Hotter means a shorter peak wavelength: which end of the visible spectrum is that?

questions.question: Which physical quantity is measured in light-years?
questions.explanation: A light-year is the length of the path light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion km. Despite the word 'year' it is not a unit of time.
questions.hintText: Multiply the speed of light by one year: what kind of quantity do you get?

questions.question: In the photoelectric effect, what does light knock out of a metal surface?
questions.explanation: Each photon gives its energy to one electron in the metal. If that energy is larger than the work function, the electron leaves the surface.
